# Environmental Gram-negatives: pseudomonads, vibrios and Burkholderia

> *A tap in a hospital ward, a flooded field and a well contaminated with faeces are the sources of
> three dangerous infections. None of these bacteria needs a human host, and the traits that keep each
> one alive in water or soil decide what it does to a patient.*

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Learning objectives
- Sort the environmental Gram-negatives by how they make ATP, by salt tolerance and by where they
  live, and state what each trait predicts about how a person meets them.
- Explain why *Pseudomonas aeruginosa* resists many drugs and disinfectants before it acquires any
  new gene, and why it damages tissue whose barrier or local defence has failed.
- Explain how *Burkholderia pseudomallei* reaches the body from soil and surface water, why diabetes
  is the commonest host factor, and what its survival inside phagocytes means for relapse.
- Explain how one toxin of *Vibrio cholerae* produces diarrhoea severe enough to kill within hours,
  and why replacing fluid and salts treats it.
- Name the host, setting and route that let each main organism cause disease.
- Tell *P. aeruginosa* from *B. pseudomallei* by setting, host factor, life inside cells and latency.
:::

## The group {#sec-egn-group}

### The group in one sentence {#sec-egn-sentence}

Environmental Gram-negatives are Gram-negative rods whose home is water, wet soil or the sea, and
which reach people from that home rather than from another person. Most of the six questions have one
answer for the whole group; its members differ mainly in which part of the environment they live in
and in how they damage the host.

| Question | Answer for the environmental Gram-negatives |
|---|---|
| What is it built from? | A Gram-negative envelope: thin peptidoglycan under an outer membrane whose outer face is lipopolysaccharide (LPS); straight rods in *Pseudomonas* and *Burkholderia*, curved rods in the vibrios; flagella for swimming |
| How does it get energy? | *Pseudomonas* and *Burkholderia* cannot ferment sugars and depend on respiration, usually with oxygen; the vibrios respire or ferment, and tolerate salt. All of them are oxidase positive, so the oxidase test, which detects a respiratory enzyme, separates the whole group from the gut Gram-negative rods such as *Escherichia coli* (see [*A map of the bacteria*](bacteria-map.qmd#sec-map-habitat)) |
| How does it copy itself and change? | Binary fission; several of them resist many antibacterial drugs as a property of the species, and acquire further resistance by mutation and gene transfer |
| Where does it live, and how does it spread? | Water, plumbing, wet soil and the sea; people meet these bacteria through broken skin, in inhaled spray, in contaminated drinking water or in seafood. Spread between people is unusual, although *P. aeruginosa* passes from patient to patient in hospital on hands and equipment, and the faeces of a patient infected with *V. cholerae* contaminate the water that infects the next person |
| How does damage happen? | *P. aeruginosa* multiplies in tissue whose barrier has failed; *B. pseudomallei* survives inside phagocytes and forms abscesses; *V. cholerae* acts through a single toxin on the gut lining; and in all of them LPS drives inflammation once they reach the blood |
| What does it have that my cells lack? | A peptidoglycan wall and the proteins that build it, although the outer membrane and pumps in the cell membrane keep many drugs away from those targets |

Life outside a host makes these bacteria hardy. They need few nutrients, tolerate a wide range of
temperatures and survive in water for long periods, so they persist in plumbing, in equipment and in
soil, and they grow overnight on ordinary media in air. Their envelope carries LPS, so the
inflammation that follows their arrival in the blood is the inflammation of any Gram-negative
infection (see [*How bacteria are built and get
energy*](bacteria-build-energy.qmd#sec-bact-envelope)).

*Pseudomonas* and *Burkholderia* cannot ferment sugars, so they depend on respiration and do best in
wet places that air reaches: wet surfaces, damp soil and standing water (see [*A map of the
bacteria*](bacteria-map.qmd#sec-map-habitat) and [*How bacteria are built and get
energy*](bacteria-build-energy.qmd#sec-bact-oxygen)). Oxygen is not the only acceptor available to
them: *P. aeruginosa* can respire with nitrate instead, which lets it grow in thick, oxygen-poor
mucus and in the gut of some hospital patients. Neither organism competes well with the fermenters of
the colon, so neither is a resident of the gut.

### Sorting the group {#sec-egn-key}

Three traits separate the members of the group:

- Whether the organism can ferment sugars, which separates the strict respirers from the vibrios
- Salt tolerance, which marks the organisms of the sea
- Where in the environment it lives, which decides how a person meets it

::: {.concept-tree}
[Sorting the environmental Gram-negatives]{.tree-title}

- Cannot ferment sugars; depends on respiration, usually with oxygen
  - Water and moist surfaces, including hospital sinks, taps and equipment: *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*
  - Wet soil and surface water in the tropics: *Burkholderia pseudomallei*
- Ferments as well as respiring, and tolerates salt: the vibrios, curved rods
  - Fresh or brackish water contaminated with human faeces: *Vibrio cholerae*
  - Warm seawater, and the shellfish that filter it: *Vibrio vulnificus*
  - Coastal seawater, in raw or undercooked seafood: *Vibrio parahaemolyticus*
:::

Where the organism lives predicts how a person meets it and what follows:

| Where it lives | How a person meets it | What follows |
|---|---|---|
| Water and moist surfaces, including hospital sinks, taps, drains and equipment | Through skin lost to a burn, along a device, or into an airway held open by a tube | Infection of damaged tissue and of devices; healthy tissue is seldom harmed |
| Wet soil and surface water in the tropics | Through broken skin, inhaled in spray and dust, or swallowed, mostly in the rainy season | Pneumonia, abscesses in several organs and spread in the blood, above all in people with diabetes |
| Fresh or brackish water contaminated with human faeces | Swallowed in water or food | Profuse watery diarrhoea from a toxin, and death from dehydration within hours if fluid is not replaced |
| Warm seawater, and raw or undercooked seafood | Swallowed, or through a wound exposed to seawater | **Gastroenteritis**, inflammation of the stomach and intestines that causes vomiting, diarrhoea or both; with *V. vulnificus*, severe wound infection and spread to the blood, especially in chronic liver disease |

Work through the key from how the organism makes ATP, and read at each branch what the trait predicts
about the organism.

## Main organisms {#sec-egn-main}

### *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*: water, biofilm and natural resistance {#sec-egn-pseudomonas}

*P. aeruginosa* is a Gram-negative rod of water and moist surfaces. It grows in sinks, taps, drains,
the water in flower vases, humidifiers and ventilator tubing, and in solutions of disinfectant that
have become contaminated, and its colonies make a blue-green pigment that can colour the pus of an
infected wound.

Three features of the cell resist antibacterial drugs and disinfectants before the organism acquires
anything. Its outer membrane admits fewer molecules than that of *E. coli*; **efflux pumps**,
membrane proteins that expel drugs from the cell, remove much of what does enter; and an enzyme
encoded in its chromosome, a beta-lactamase, destroys several beta-lactam drugs. Resistance that is
a property of a whole species in this way is **intrinsic resistance**, and strains
acquire further resistance by mutation and gene transfer (see [*How bacteria copy themselves and
change*](bacterial-genetics.qmd#sec-gen-mechanisms)). On a surface the bacteria grow as a
**biofilm**, a community of microbes embedded in a shared matrix on a surface, which shelters them
from drugs and from phagocytes (see [*How bacteria are built and get
energy*](bacteria-build-energy.qmd#sec-bact-extras)).

::: {.callout-important}
## Is resistance always something a bacterium acquires?
Resistance is widely assumed to be acquired strain by strain wherever antibacterial drugs have been
used heavily, and much of it is: MRSA carries an acquired gene for an altered drug target (see [*How
bacteria copy themselves and change*](bacterial-genetics.qmd#sec-gen-mechanisms)).

Much of the resistance of *P. aeruginosa* belongs to the species itself, so a strain from a patient
who has never been treated already resists several drugs that act well on Enterobacterales.
Treatment starts from a shorter list of drugs than for a gut Gram-negative rod, and acquired
resistance shortens that list further.
:::

*P. aeruginosa* seldom harms intact tissue, and it is an opportunistic pathogen in the sense used in
[*Microbes and their hosts*](../foundations/host-microbe.qmd#sec-host-opportunism): disease follows
when a barrier or a local defence has failed.

| Pattern of harm | Mechanism | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Infection of tissue that has lost its barrier | The bacteria multiply in warm, moist, damaged tissue and destroy it with secreted enzymes, and neutrophils gather | Infection of a burn; **otitis externa**, inflammation of the ear canal, after water remains in the ear |
| Infection on a surface the bacteria have colonised | Biofilm on plastic or on a lens shelters them from drugs and from phagocytes | **Keratitis**, inflammation of the cornea, in a contact lens wearer, which can destroy the cornea within days |
| Persistent infection of an airway that cannot clear its secretions | Thick mucus and biofilm hold the bacteria where neither coughing nor drugs remove them, and years of inflammation damage the airway wall | Chronic infection of the lungs in **cystic fibrosis**, an inherited disease in which the secretions of the airway are thick and difficult to clear; pneumonia in a ventilated patient |
| Spread to the blood | From infected tissue or a device the bacteria enter the blood, where LPS drives inflammation (see [*How bacteria cause damage*](bacterial-damage.qmd#sec-bdam-endotoxin)) | **Sepsis**, life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection, in a patient with extensive burns or with too few neutrophils |

Three conditions let *P. aeruginosa* cause disease:

| | Condition | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Who (host) | A person whose barrier or local defence has failed: extensive burns, cystic fibrosis, an airway held open by a tube, a cornea under a contact lens; or a person whose neutrophils are too few, as after cancer chemotherapy | Each has lost the skin, the mucus clearance or the intact epithelium that keeps the bacteria out of tissue, or the neutrophils that kill the bacteria that get in (see [*Microbes and their hosts*](../foundations/host-microbe.qmd#sec-host-factors)) |
| Where (setting) | Moist places, including hospital sinks, taps, drains and equipment | The organism needs few nutrients and survives in water, so it persists in plumbing and on wet equipment |
| How (route) | Through skin lost to a burn, along a device or a lens, or into an airway bypassed by a tube | It multiplies in damaged tissue, and on a surface it forms biofilm, where drugs and phagocytes reach it poorly |

Step through the two routes *P. aeruginosa* takes, from hospital water into a burn and into a damaged
airway.

### *Burkholderia pseudomallei*: soil, diabetes and life inside cells {#sec-egn-burkholderia}

*B. pseudomallei* lives in wet soil and surface water across South-East Asia, including Singapore,
and northern Australia, where it is most common; it is also found across South Asia and southern
China, and is increasingly recognised elsewhere in the tropics. **Melioidosis** is infection with
this soil bacterium. Heavy rain brings the bacteria to the surface, so cases follow the rainy season,
and they reach people in three ways: through broken skin in contact with soil or water, inhaled in
spray and dust, and swallowed in contaminated water. Most illness begins one to three weeks after
such an exposure. Diabetes, which impairs neutrophil function, is the commonest host factor; others
are hazardous alcohol use and chronic kidney disease, and some patients have none of them (see
[*Microbes and their hosts*](../foundations/host-microbe.qmd#sec-host-case), where two gardeners who
worked the same wet soil had different outcomes).

Phagocytes engulf *B. pseudomallei* and it survives inside them, so it grows both inside and outside
host cells (see [*A map of the bacteria*](bacteria-map.qmd#sec-map-where)). Bacteria inside cells are
out of reach of antibodies and of drugs that do not enter cells, so treatment continues for months
and the infection can relapse. The same shelter allows a **latent infection**, persistence of an
organism in a silent state, with the possibility of reactivation (see [*Microbes and their
hosts*](../foundations/host-microbe.qmd#sec-host-courses)); disease after years of latency is
uncommon but well documented. The organism is also naturally resistant to several classes of
antibacterial drug, so the choice of treatment is narrow from the start. In the laboratory its
colonies can be mistaken for a contaminant or misidentified, and it can infect laboratory staff, so
the clinician warns the laboratory when melioidosis is suspected.

| Pattern of harm | Mechanism | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Infection at the site of entry | The bacteria multiply in the tissue they enter, and pus collects | A skin abscess or ulcer where wet soil entered a cut |
| Pneumonia | Inhaled bacteria multiply in the alveoli, and bacteria carried in the blood can settle there as well | Fever and cough in a man who worked wet soil after heavy rain |
| Abscesses in several organs | Carried in the blood, the bacteria survive inside the phagocytes of the organs they reach, and pus collects there | Abscesses in the liver and spleen in a patient with fever and weight loss |
| Sepsis | Large numbers of bacteria in the blood, with LPS and other bacterial components driving inflammation | Hypotension and organ failure within days of the first symptoms |
| Disease after a latent period | Bacteria persist inside cells without causing illness and multiply again when defences weaken | Melioidosis beginning years after the person left the region where the organism lives, an uncommon pattern |

Three conditions let *B. pseudomallei* cause disease:

| | Condition | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Who (host) | Most often a person with diabetes, above all when it is poorly controlled, and sometimes one with hazardous alcohol use or chronic kidney disease; some patients have no such factor at all | Diabetes impairs neutrophil function, so the bacteria that enter are cleared less well |
| Where (setting) | Wet soil and surface water in the tropics, above all in South-East Asia, including Singapore, and northern Australia, especially in the rainy season | The organism lives in the environment and needs no host, and heavy rain brings it to the surface |
| How (route) | Through broken skin in soil or water, inhaled in spray and dust, or swallowed | Once inside, it survives within phagocytes, which carries it in the blood to other organs and lets it persist |

Step through the two routes *B. pseudomallei* takes: through the skin to the organs, and inhaled, with
disease years later.

### *Vibrio cholerae*: one toxin and litres of water {#sec-egn-vibrio}

*V. cholerae* is a curved Gram-negative rod of fresh and brackish water, which ferments as well as
respiring and tolerates salt. **Cholera** is the illness it causes: profuse watery diarrhoea, from a
single toxin, that can kill by dehydration within hours. Only strains carrying the gene for that
toxin cause it, and most *V. cholerae* in the environment do not. Spread is faecal–oral (see
[*Transmission, outbreaks and One
Health*](../foundations/transmission-outbreaks.qmd#sec-trans-routes)): faeces from an infected person
reach drinking water or food, and the next person swallows the bacteria. Stomach acid kills most of
them, so a large inoculum must arrive, and contaminated water and food matter more than contact
between people (see [*Microbes and their hosts*](../foundations/host-microbe.qmd#sec-host-factors)).

::: {.example}
Deaths from cholera in London in 1854 clustered around a single water pump, which was evidence that
the cause is swallowed in water (see [*Transmission, outbreaks and One
Health*](../foundations/transmission-outbreaks.qmd#sec-trans-case)).
:::

The bacteria stay in the lumen of the small intestine. They attach to its lining and release a single
toxin, which enters the lining cells and raises the concentration of cyclic AMP in them (see [*How
bacteria cause damage*](bacterial-damage.qmd#sec-bdam-exotoxins)). The cells then secrete chloride,
and water and other salts follow it into the gut: in severe cholera, up to a litre an hour. The stool
is watery and pale, flecked with mucus, with no blood, and there is usually no fever, because the
wall of the gut is never invaded.

Death comes from the loss of fluid and salts, so treatment is their replacement, by mouth where the
patient can drink and into a vein when the circulation is failing. A solution of glucose and salts is
absorbed while the toxin is still acting, because the transport that carries sodium into the lining
cells alongside glucose keeps working. Antibacterial drugs shorten the illness and the period of
shedding, and they do nothing for the volume already lost.

| Pattern of harm | Mechanism | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Loss of fluid and salts into the gut | The toxin raises cyclic AMP in the cells lining the small intestine, which secrete chloride, and water and other salts follow | Watery diarrhoea, pale and flecked with mucus, beginning abruptly and continuing for days |
| Dehydration and shock | Fluid leaves the circulation faster than the patient can drink to replace it | Collapse within hours of the first stool in an untreated patient |

Three conditions let *V. cholerae* cause disease:

| | Condition | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Who (host) | Anyone who swallows enough bacteria; the harm falls hardest on young children and on anyone unable to drink as fast as the fluid is lost | Fluid loss at this rate empties a small circulation first, and recovery depends on replacing what is lost |
| Where (setting) | Water or food contaminated with human faeces, where clean water and sanitation have failed | The bacteria live in fresh and brackish water, and faeces from patients return them to it |
| How (route) | Swallowed; the bacteria remain in the lumen of the small intestine | Stomach acid kills most of them, so a large number must arrive; survivors attach to the lining and release toxin |

Step through the route *V. cholerae* takes, from contaminated water to the gut and back to the water.

## Contrast pair {#sec-egn-pairs}

### *P. aeruginosa* and *B. pseudomallei* {#sec-egn-pair-pseudomonas-burkholderia}

Both are environmental Gram-negative rods that depend on respiration, and both are naturally
resistant to many antibacterial drugs. Compare them feature by feature before reading the principle.

## Beyond the main organisms {#sec-egn-beyond}

### Supporting organisms {#sec-egn-supporting}

| Organism | Where it lives | What separates it | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|---|
| *V. vulnificus* | Warm seawater, and the shellfish that filter it | Needs salt to grow, and multiplies fast in tissue | Infection of a wound exposed to seawater, which can destroy skin and the tissue beneath it within hours, and sepsis after raw shellfish; both are most dangerous in people with chronic liver disease |
| *V. parahaemolyticus* | Coastal seawater and seafood | Needs salt; stays in the gut | A common cause of diarrhoea and abdominal pain hours to a day after raw or undercooked seafood |

### Later in the course {#sec-egn-later}

| Organism | Where it comes up again |
|---|---|
| *P. aeruginosa* | Healthcare-associated infection, burns and intensive care; respiratory medicine (cystic fibrosis and ventilated patients); ophthalmology (keratitis); anti-pseudomonal drugs in pharmacology |
| *B. pseudomallei* | Infectious diseases in Singapore and the region (melioidosis); infection in diabetes in endocrinology |
| *V. cholerae* | Gastroenterology (acute watery diarrhoea and rehydration); public health (water, sanitation and outbreak control) |
| *V. vulnificus* | Emergency medicine and surgery (severe wound infection); hepatology |
| *V. parahaemolyticus* | Gastroenterology and food safety |
